newsitem.title: TOGO: Zaire's warring parties agree to talks, no date. [CORRECTED 2:29 GMT 28/3]
newsitem.headline: Zaire's warring parties agree to talks, no date. [CORRECTED 2:29 GMT 28/3]

text.p: Zaire's warring parties, brought together by Organisation of African Unity (OAU) leaders at a special summit in Togo, have agreed to hold talks -- but have not fixed the date.

The summit, an attempt to streamline a host of initiatives to contain the crisis at the volatile heart of Africa, closed after calling on the two sides to hold immediate talks leading to a ceasefire -- a moral victory for Laurent Kabila's rebels.
It urged all players to throw their weight behind a five point peace plan formulated by U.N. and OAU special representative Mohamed Sahnoun.
But despite intensive efforts on the sidelines by host President Gnassingbe Eyadema and the presidents of Nigeria and Cameroon, the various leaders dispersed without any announcement on dates.
"The two delegations have reiterated their commitment to accept the principle of a ceasefire and the principle of negotiations," a statement on the parallel talks said.

A date for negotiations and a ceasefire will be announced by the OAU, the U.N. and in Togo's capital Lome, in Zaire's capital Kinshasa and rebel headquarters in Goma after the delegations had consulted their respective parties, it added.

The rebels, who control one fifth of the sprawling Central African nation, took up arms in October vowing to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko while the veteran leader was in Europe recovering from prostate cancer surgery.

The revolt has weakened Mobutu's grip on the former Belgian colony he has dominated since seizing power in 1965. Ordinary Zaireans, impoverished by three decades of Mobutu's rule, are eager for change -- from whatever direction it comes.
Kabila's popularity has risen with each battlefield victory and many people in Kinshasa's teeming suburbs say they would welcome him with open arms.
The OAU summit gave the rebels, who had called for talks before any truce (Corrects to make clear that talks were to come first),
their first major international platform.
Bizima Karaha, Kabila's foreign affairs strategist, told a news conference on the sidelines of the summit that talks were imminent and South Africa or Togo were likely venues.

"We are very excited to learn that for the first time the people from Kinshasa have decided to agree on a starting of the negotiations which are going to be in a very few days to come," he said. "We are ready to go in any country as long as those Zaireans are serious."
He said the rebels were ready to agree a truce, but the question was with whom as there was a "political vacuum".

But Karaha said Mobutu, who returned home on Friday after fresh cancer treatment in Europe, remained a player. "There are some people who have a little power (left), in particular Mobutu and we would like to negotiate with him," he added.
Karaha said that Kabila would not negotiate in person as the rebels had a special team to do that.
Kakudji and Karaha said they shook hands with the representatives of the central authorities late on Wednesday in the presence of Eyadema and U.N. secretary General Kofi Annan.
But there were no negotiations as such, with the rebel representatives saying the Kinshasa delegation had no mandate.

France and the United States, accused of supporting opposite sides, are among Western nations who have sent troops to the region to evacuate their nationals if peace efforts collapse and violence erupts in Kinshasa.
They put on a show of unity, lobbying jointly for a truce and talks.
